book: Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code
author: Martin Fowler

principles.rule: Refactor in small, behavior-preserving steps; run the tests after each step. Never change behavior and structure at the same time.
checks: each refactoring step keeps tests green
no functional change inside a refactoring step

principles.rule: Maintain self-testing code; do not refactor without reliable tests covering the area being changed. Add a test before fixing a bug.
checks: bug reproduced by a test first

principles.rule: Wear one hat at a time: separate adding functionality from refactoring (ideally in separate commits).
checks: feature changes and refactors not mixed in one commit

principles.rule: Treat code smells as signals to refactor: long functions, duplicated code, long parameter lists, feature envy, primitive obsession, large classes, divergent change, shotgun surgery.
checks: no long methods/large classes left untouched when edited

principles.rule: Prefer Extract Function and good naming to clarify intent rather than adding explanatory comments.
checks: complex blocks extracted into well-named functions

principles.rule: Apply the Rule of Three: remove duplication by the third occurrence.
checks: no third copy of the same logic

principles.rule: Use preparatory refactoring: when a change is hard, first refactor to make the change easy, then make it.
checks: code reshaped to simplify an upcoming change

principles.rule: Simplify conditionals: use guard clauses, decompose conditionals, and replace type-switch conditionals with polymorphism where appropriate.
